title: A peak element is one that is strictly greater than its neighbors. Given an array where neighbors differ, return the index of any peak. Assume elements outside the array are negative infinity. Run in logarithmic time.
shortTitle: Find a Peak Element: Binary Search on the Slope
keyPoints: A peak element is strictly greater than its neighbors, with boundaries treated as negative infinity.
Binary search works on an unsorted array here because the slope structure guarantees a peak exists in the uphill direction.
Compare arr[mid] with arr[mid + 1]: if climbing, move right; if descending, move left.
Use while (low < high) and set high = mid to converge two pointers to a single peak index.
The invariant is that a peak always exists within the current window because at least one boundary points uphill.
The array need not be sorted; the only requirement is that adjacent elements differ.
Time complexity is O(log n) and space complexity is O(1).

s1_definition.oneliner: Compare the middle element to its right neighbor and always walk uphill; a peak is guaranteed in that direction because boundaries are negative infinity.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Peak element** – an element strictly greater than both its neighbors, with positions outside the array treated as negative infinity.
- **Slope-based binary search** – compare `arr[mid]` with `arr[mid + 1]` to determine the slope direction at mid.
- **Climbing** – if `arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1]`, a peak lies to the right, so `low = mid + 1`.
- **Descending** – if `arr[mid] > arr[mid + 1]`, mid is a peak or a peak lies to the left, so `high = mid`.
- **Convergence** – use `while (low < high)`; when the pointers meet, that index is a peak. O(log n) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India charts hourly trading volume, which rises and falls like hills. The operations team wants any local high point, an hour busier than its immediate neighbors. A clerk stands at the middle hour and looks right. If the next hour is busier, the clerk walks uphill to the right because a peak must lie that way. If it is quieter, the peak is at the clerk's feet or to the left.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Array: [100, 300, 500, 400, 200, 600, 350]

Visualized as terrain:

        500          600
       / \          / \
     300   400    200   350
    /        \   /       \
  100         200        (end)

  ↑ ascending  ↓ descending  ↑ ascending  ↓ descending

Binary search on slope:
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Step 1: low=0 high=6 mid=3                   │
│   arr[3]=400 > arr[4]=200 → descending       │
│   Peak at mid or left → high = 3             │
│                                              │
│ Step 2: low=0 high=3 mid=1                   │
│   arr[1]=300 < arr[2]=500 → ascending        │
│   Peak to right → low = 2                    │
│                                              │
│ Step 3: low=2 high=3 mid=2                   │
│   arr[2]=500 > arr[3]=400 → descending       │
│   Peak at mid or left → high = 2             │
│                                              │
│ low == high == 2 → Peak found: 500           │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding a peak element is a surprising case where binary search works on an array that is not sorted at all, because the problem has a slope structure that can be exploited. On each step you compare the middle element to its immediate right neighbor. If the right neighbor is larger, you are climbing a slope, and since the array boundaries behave like negative infinity, that uphill direction must eventually turn into a peak, so you move low past the middle. If the right neighbor is smaller, then the middle is itself a peak or a peak lies to its left, so you move high to the middle.

Because you always walk toward the taller neighbor, the invariant that a peak exists somewhere inside the current window is preserved while the window halves each step, so the search converges on a peak in logarithmic time. The index mid plus one is always safe to read because the loop only runs while low is strictly less than high, which keeps the middle at least one step short of the right edge.

In Rajesh's work at the National Bank of India, the trading desk records hourly trade volumes across the day, and the monitoring dashboard flags local peak hours to investigate spikes. The volumes rise and fall unpredictably so the series is unsorted, yet this slope-based binary search finds a peak logarithmically, keeping the dashboard responsive even over long time series.

The insight to emphasize in interviews is the proof of correctness: there is always a peak within the window because at least one boundary points uphill into it, and moving toward the higher neighbor never destroys that guarantee. Being able to articulate the invariant rather than just reciting the code is what demonstrates real understanding.

Remember one sentence: compare mid to its right neighbor and always walk uphill, because a peak is guaranteed in the direction of the ascending slope.
